translation_notes: BEST FIT of the set. The script's own comment block says 'The generated turtle file should look like this:' followed by seven lines of Turtle; the ldpy island that replaces the seven g.add() calls is that comment, verbatim, as executable code -- same subjects grouped with ';', same '.' between subjects, 'a' for A

seven g.add((s, A, o)) / g.add((s, BRICK.hasPart, o)) calls merged into one 'g += g{...}'; the per-sensor loop body's three g.add() calls merged into one island with ';' (the loop, the tuple unpacking and the sensors list are untouched Python, the terms interpolated as {sensor} {brick_type} {units} {location})

brickschema's Graph.add((s, p, [(p1,o1), (p2,o2)])) extension -- a library-specific sugar for a blank node, flagged in the source by the comment 'this nifty syntax requires brickschema>=0.3.2a1' -- becomes the standard Turtle blank-node property list 'bldg:room_1 brick:area [ brick:value {..} ; brick:hasUnit unit:M2 ]'. Same triples, no library extension needed. The room_area / floor_area variables are absorbed (they existed only to build the blank node); the stale comment is kept verbatim as required by the faithfulness rules

LIMIT FOUND: the typed literal could NOT become an island. '"40"^^xsd:double' builds Literal('40', datatype=XSD.double), which rdflib re-normalises to lexical form '40.0' -- a different RDF term from the original's Literal(40, datatype=XSD.double), whose lexical form is '40'. The graphs would not be isomorphic, so the value stays a {Literal(40, datatype=XSD.double)} interpolation. (Same for 1000.) This is an rdflib lexical-normalisation asymmetry, not an ldpy bug, but it means a mechanical Literal(n, datatype=t) -> "n"^^t rule is unsound

LIMIT FOUND: one of the five sensor rows keeps the Python form -- BLDG["pm2.5_sensor"], BRICK["PM2.5_Sensor"], UNIT["MicroGM-PER-M3"] -- because outside a g{} island a prefixed-name local part may only use the intersection of Python identifier characters and Turtle's PN_CHARS: '.' would read as attribute access and '-' as subtraction. Turtle itself has no such problem, and the file the script writes contains exactly 'bldg:pm2.5_sensor a brick:PM2.5_Sensor ; brick:hasUnit unit:MicroGM-PER-M3' -- ldpy can read those names back but cannot write them outside an island. Inside the island they would be legal, which is why the other four rows could be moved but this one could not

LIMIT FOUND: BLDG = Namespace('http://example.com#') is kept ALONGSIDE '@prefix bldg: <http://example.com#> .' because g.bind('bldg', BLDG) needs a runtime Namespace object and @prefix is a transpile-time declaration. The example IRI is therefore written twice. Dropping g.bind was not an option: the script serialises the model to Turtle, so the prefix binding is observable
'from brickschema.namespaces import A, OWL, BRICK, UNIT, XSD' is kept verbatim although A becomes unused (absorbed by Turtle's 'a') -- only import lines may be adjusted, and only for executability

context shims (identical for both sides, resolved by import path so no import line changed): local packages brickschema/ (namespaces.py copied from the BrickSchema/py-brickschema checkout; graph.py transcribing the prefix binding, load_file and the list-of-pairs add) and brick_tq_shacl/ (infer is a no-op stand-in for the topquadrant SHACL engine)

'../../Brick.ttl' is a generated artefact absent from the BrickSchema/Brick checkout, so the shim's load_file skips a missing file: the room-type query and the two closing SPARQL queries return no rows, identically on both sides. The model-building part of the region -- all 36 RDF operations -- is fully exercised: both sides produce the same 29-triple graph, and perturbing a single predicate in the island makes the driver report the graphs non-isomorphic
air_quality_sensor_example.ttl is written by the region itself into the example directory when the driver runs
